title: Machine Learning Model
shortDefinition: A system trained on data to find patterns and make predictions without explicit programming.
definition: A machine learning model is a system trained on data to find patterns and make predictions or decisions, without being explicitly programmed with rules for every scenario. Instead of writing if-then logic for every case, a machine learning model learns the relationship between inputs and outputs from historical examples, then applies that learned relationship to new, unseen data.

sections.title: Types of machine learning models
sections.description: Supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning are the major approaches.

content.text: The major categories of machine learning are supervised learning (training on labeled examples where the correct answer is known, used for classification and regression tasks like fraud detection or demand forecasting), unsupervised learning (finding patterns or groupings in data without labeled answers, used for customer segmentation or anomaly detection), and reinforcement learning (learning through trial and reward, used in recommendation systems and certain optimization problems). Most business applications use supervised learning, since labeled historical outcome data is typically available.

content.title: Most business use cases are supervised
content.text: If you have historical examples with known outcomes (e.g., past customers and whether they churned), you can build a supervised model to predict future outcomes.

sections.title: How to know if you need a custom model vs. an LLM

content.text: Not every prediction problem needs an LLM. If your task is structured numerical prediction — credit risk scoring, demand forecasting, fraud detection, churn prediction — a purpose-built machine learning model (trained on PyTorch, TensorFlow, or Scikit-learn) typically outperforms an LLM-based approach on accuracy, cost, and latency. LLMs excel at language understanding and generation tasks; traditional ML models excel at structured prediction from tabular or numerical data. Many production systems combine both.

content.title: Use a traditional ML model when:
items: You have structured tabular or numerical data (e.g., customer demographics, transaction history).
You need a highly interpretable prediction (e.g., credit decision with SHAP explanations).
Your prediction task is well-defined with a clear numeric or categorical output.
You need low latency and low cost per prediction.
You have hundreds to thousands of labeled historical examples.

content.title: Use an LLM when:
items: Your task involves language understanding, generation, or summarization.
You need to reason about text, documents, or conversational inputs.
You don't have a large labeled dataset but still need semantic reasoning.
Your problem is open-ended or requires creative output.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of machine learning models

content.text: Machine learning models are powerful but have inherent risks. They are only as good as the data they're trained on — garbage in, garbage out. They can overfit to training data, fail to generalize to new environments, introduce bias from historical data, and degrade over time as the world changes. Without proper monitoring, they can produce erroneous predictions without warning.

items: Data dependency: model quality depends entirely on training data quality and representativeness.
Overfitting: models can memorize training data and fail on new data.
Concept drift: model performance degrades as the real-world data distribution changes.
Bias: models can amplify historical biases in training data.
Black-box complexity: deep models can be difficult to interpret.
Maintenance burden: models require ongoing monitoring, retraining, and updates.
Infrastructure cost: training and inference at scale require significant compute resources.

content.title: Important
content.text: A machine learning model is not a 'set it and forget it' asset. Continuous monitoring, periodic retraining, and regular evaluation are essential for production-grade systems.

sections.title: Best practices for custom ML model development

content.text: Building a reliable production ML model requires rigorous data handling, careful model selection, and ongoing monitoring. The following practices can help ensure your model delivers measurable value.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Start with a clear, measurable business metric (e.g., reduce false positives by 30%).
Collect and clean a representative dataset with historical examples.
Split data into train, validation, and test sets (e.g., 60/20/20).
Start with a simple baseline model before moving to complex architectures.
Use cross-validation to detect overfitting early.
Build SHAP/LIME explainability to understand model decisions.
Deploy with monitoring (MLflow) for accuracy, latency, and drift detection.
Set up automated retraining pipelines triggered by drift or new data arrival.
Version control all data, models, and preprocessing code.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure model performance on the held-out test set before deployment. That's the only number that reflects real-world generalizability.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about machine learning models

items.question: What's the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
items.answer: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples where the correct answer is known (used for prediction tasks like fraud detection); unsupervised learning finds patterns without labeled answers (used for segmentation or anomaly detection).

items.question: How much data do we need to build a custom machine learning model?
items.answer: This varies significantly by task complexity, but most useful models need at least hundreds to thousands of labeled historical examples. ClickMasters assesses your specific data during Discovery.

items.question: How do you prevent the model from just memorizing the training data?
items.answer: ClickMasters uses proper train/validation/test data splitting and cross-validation techniques specifically to detect and prevent overfitting before a model is deployed.

items.question: Will we be able to understand why the model made a specific prediction?
items.answer: Yes, ClickMasters builds SHAP/LIME explainability tooling as standard for any model influencing consequential decisions like credit, hiring, or claims.

items.question: How long does a custom machine learning project take?
items.answer: 10–28 weeks depending on use case complexity and monitoring/retraining infrastructure requirements.

items.question: What happens if the model's accuracy degrades over time after deployment?
items.answer: ClickMasters builds monitoring infrastructure (via MLflow) to detect performance drift, with retraining available as an ongoing service.

items.question: What is the difference between a machine learning model and a deep learning model?
items.answer: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers (deep architectures). Deep learning excels at unstructured data like images, audio, and text, while traditional ML models (like random forests or linear regression) are often better for structured tabular data.

items.question: Can a machine learning model be combined with an LLM?
items.answer: Yes — many production systems use a traditional ML model for structured predictions (e.g., risk scores) and an LLM for natural language explanation or natural language interaction. The ML model provides the numeric prediction; the LLM provides the human-readable reason.

items.question: What is model drift and why does it matter?
items.answer: Model drift (also called concept drift) occurs when the real-world data distribution changes, making the model's predictions less accurate over time. Without monitoring, you won't know your model is degrading until it's affecting business outcomes.

items.question: Do we need to retrain the model regularly, and if so, how often?
items.answer: Retraining frequency depends on how fast your data distribution changes. Some models are retrained daily; others quarterly. ClickMasters monitors performance and alerts you when drift crosses a threshold, triggering a retraining cycle when needed.
